# Insulin

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Endocrinology > Relevant pharmacology > Insulin*

[Original Article Link](/library/Gm0BSg)

---

## Summary

Insulin is an <u>anabolic</u> <u>peptide hormone</u> that is produced and secreted from <u>β cells</u> located in the <u>islets of Langerhans</u> of the <u>pancreas</u>. By modulating <u>glucose absorption</u> from the blood, insulin lowers blood <u>glucose</u> levels. Further important metabolic functions of insulin include the promotion of <u>carbohydrate</u>, <u>amino acid</u>, and fat storage in the <u>liver</u>, <u>skeletal muscle</u>, and <u>adipose tissues</u>. There are several insulin analogs (e.g., <u>insulin glargine</u>) with a different molecular structure but similar properties to human insulin, with differences mainly in the onset, peak, and duration of action. <u>Insulin therapy</u> is an important part of treatment for individuals with no or insufficient insulin production (e.g., <u>diabetes mellitus</u>, <u>gestational diabetes</u>). It is crucial that patients receiving <u>insulin therapy</u> undergo in-depth training to prevent potentially life-threatening conditions such as <u>hypoglycemia</u> as a result of an insulin overdose or <u>drug interactions</u>.




See also “<u>Antihyperglycemic treatment of diabetes mellitus</u>” and “<u>Inpatient management of hyperglycemia</u>.”




For synthesis and regulation of insulin see “<u>Endocrine pancreas</u>.”

## Pharmacodynamics

### Insulin function and metabolic effects




* Insulin binds to insulin <u>receptors</u> (a type of <u>tyrosine kinase receptor</u>) located in various tissues in the body (e.g., <u>liver</u>, <u>skeletal muscle</u>, <u>adipose tissue</u>, <u>cell membranes</u>). [[4]](/library/w1XhQC)

* In target tissues, insulin acts as an <u>anabolic</u> <u>hormone</u>.





| Metabolic actions of insulin |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | Increases | Decreases |
| <u>Carbohydrate</u> metabolism | <br><br>* Carrier-mediated uptake of <u>glucose</u> into <u>skeletal muscle</u> and <u>adipose tissue</u> cells<br><br>* <u>Glycogenesis</u> in muscle and <u>liver</u><br><br>* <u>Glycolysis</u> in adipose and muscle<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Glycogenolysis</u><br><br>* <u>Gluconeogenesis</u> via dephosphorylation of <u>fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase</u>, catalyzed by <u>protein phosphatase 1</u>, which is activated by insulin. [[5]](/library/B1XzQC)<br><br>* Production and release of <u>glucagon</u> [[6]](/library/y1XdjC)<br><br><br> |
| Lipid metabolism | <br>* Lipid synthesis and <u>triglyceride</u> storage in <u>adipose tissue</u>  [[7]](/library/C1XqQC)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Lipolysis</u> in <u>adipose tissue</u>  [[8]](/library/x1XEQC)<br><br>* <u>Ketogenesis</u><br><br><br> |
| <u>Protein metabolism</u> | <br><br>* <u>Protein synthesis</u> in <u>muscle tissue</u> [[9]](/library/91XNQC)<br><br>* Uptake of <u>amino acids</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Proteolysis<br><br> |





#### Other physiologic actions of insulin




* Cellular uptake of <u>potassium</u>  [[10]](/library/XdX9oC)

* <u>Sodium</u> retention by the <u>kidney</u> [[11]](/library/VdXGKC)

* Ovarian <u>androgen</u> hypersecretion  [[12]](/library/UdXb6C)

* Decreased fibrinolytic activity  [[13]](/library/2dXT6C)

* Secretion of <u>gastric acid</u> [[14]](/library/fdXk6C)

* Cell growth and differentiation  [[15]](/library/TdX66C)[[16]](/library/gdXF6C)





### Cellular and insulin-mediated uptake of <u>glucose</u>




* <u>Glucose</u> may enter cells throughout the body via a variety of transporters.

* Different tissue types have unique <u>glucose transporters</u> (e.g., <u>GLUT1</u>, <u>GLUT2</u>, <u>GLUT3</u>, <u>GLUT4</u>, and <u>GLUT5</u>), some of which are insulin-dependent and some of which are insulin-independent.

* See “Important <u>glucose transporters</u>” in "<u>Carbohydrates</u>.”

## Indications

* <u>Type 1 diabetes mellitus</u> [[2]](/library/UIWbX50)

* <u>Type 2 diabetes mellitus</u> [[18]](/library/mdXVqC)[[19]](/library/5dXiqC)

* Indicated if weight normalization, physical activity, and noninsulin <u>antidiabetic drugs</u> do not keep blood <u>glucose</u> levels in the target range.

* Patients with <u>end-stage renal failure</u> should have doses of insulin  titrated according to the <u>glomerular filtration rate</u>. [[20]](/library/MdXMqC)

* <u>Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency</u> with secondary <u>diabetes</u>

* <u>Gestational diabetes mellitus</u>

* Acute <u>hyperkalemia</u>: A drip containing <u>regular insulin</u> and a solution of <u>glucose</u> reduces blood <u>potassium</u> levels.

* See “<u>Insulin therapy</u>” in “<u>Diabetes mellitus</u>” and “<u>Inpatient management of hyperglycemia</u>.”

---

## Adverse effects

* <u>Hypoglycemia</u>  [[21]](/library/4dX3JC)

* Weight gain  [[22]](/library/OdXIJC)

* <u>Lipodystrophy</u> at the injection site  [[23]](/library/ldXvJC)

* <u>Hypokalemia</u>

* Allergic or <u>hypersensitivity reactions</u>

* <u>Edema</u>  [[24]](/library/QdXupC)

* <u>Pain</u> and <u>erythema</u> at the injection site




We list the most important adverse effects. The selection is not exhaustive.

## Insulin regimens

### General principles




* <u>Insulin regimens</u> should be tailored individually to each patient.

* Treatment of <u>T1DM</u> requires <u>intensive insulin therapy</u> with a multi injection regimen or <u>insulin pump</u>.

* There are a variety of options for patients with <u>T2DM</u>.

* Certain <u>diabetes medications</u> (e.g., <u>sulfonylureas</u>) should be stopped when <u>insulin therapy</u> is started.

* Hospital standards vary; specialists should be involved early.





> [!WARNING]
> Not all <u>noninsulin diabetes medications</u> can be combined with insulin. Combination therapy with insulin and <u>sulfonylureas</u> should be avoided because of the risk of <u>hypoglycemia</u> and increased mortality! Once insulin is started, consider tapering and eventual discontinuation of <u>sulfonylureas</u>. Insulin combined with <u>pioglitazone</u> increases the risk of <u>edema</u>, weight gain, and <u>congestive heart failure</u>. <u>Metformin</u> is usually continued.




### Basal insulin regimens [[28]](/library/Tud6q70)




* Description: Basal insulin is added to an oral <u>diabetes medication</u> regimen.

* Indication: : initiated if there are <u>indications for insulin therapy in T2DM</u> (e.g., <u>T2DM</u> with persistently elevated <u>A1C</u> levels despite adequate treatment with noninsulin <u>antidiabetics</u>)

* Treatment options

* Once-daily injection (recommended starting regimen)

* <u>Long-acting insulin</u> (e.g., <u>glargine</u>) OR bedtime <u>NPH insulin</u>

* Starting dose: 10 units/day OR 0.1–0.2 units/kg/day

* Twice-daily <u>NPH insulin</u>: Consider for patients not meeting their glycemic target with bedtime <u>NPH</u>.
* Starting dose: 80% of the previously prescribed bedtime <u>NPH insulin</u> dose, with two-thirds given in the morning and one-third at bedtime

* <u>Titration</u>

* Adjust according to glycemic monitoring.

* Levels above target: Increase insulin dose by 2 units every 3 days until preprandial <u>fasting</u> <u>glucose</u> target is met.

* If <u>hypoglycemia</u> due to <u>insulin therapy</u> occurs, reduce insulin dose by 10–20%.

* If treatment is insufficient despite adjustments, intensify therapy by either:

* Adding prandial insulin

* Switching to <u>mixed insulin regimen</u>





### Prandial insulin [[28]](/library/Tud6q70)




* Description

* Short-acting, rapid-acting, ultra-rapid-acting, or inhaled human insulin administered before major meals in patients already on a <u>basal insulin regimen</u>

* Prandial insulin can be added before one meal (the largest meal of the day) or several meals.

* Indication

* <u>T2DM</u> that is not adequately controlled with basal insulin alone

* Part of <u>full basal-bolus insulin regimen</u> (e.g., in <u>T1DM</u>)

* Starting dose

* Basal insulin injections are continued at the previous dose.

* Prandial insulin dosed at 4 units (or 10% of daily basal insulin dose) before chosen meals.

* <u>Titration</u>: Adjust according to glycemic monitoring.

* Increase prandial insulin dose by 1–2 units (or 10–15%) twice weekly until preprandial <u>fasting</u> <u>glucose</u> target is met.

* If <u>hypoglycemia</u> occurs, reduce the corresponding prandial insulin dose by 10–20%.





### Mixed insulin regimens [[28]](/library/Tud6q70)




* Description

* Twice-daily injections of a fixed combination of <u>NPH</u> mixed with either <u>short-acting insulin</u> or <u>rapid-acting insulin</u>; can be self-mixed or premixed

* Administered as two-thirds of the total daily dose 30 minutes before breakfast and one-third 30 minutes before dinner.

* Simple regimens that require minimal patient education and time

* Indication: Consider for patients with <u>T2DM</u> who are not meeting glycemic targets with a <u>basal insulin regimen</u>.

* Starting dose

* Self-mixed split insulin

* Calculate 80% of the current <u>NPH</u> dose.

* Add 4 units (or 10% of the <u>NPH</u> dose) of short-acting or <u>rapid-acting insulin</u> per injection.

* <u>Premixed insulin</u>: Use the same previous total insulin dose (i.e., the same as for the twice-daily <u>NPH</u> regimen).

* <u>Titration</u>

* Adjust according to glycemic target.

* If treatment results remain inadequate, consider a full basal-bolus regimen.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Mixed insulin regimens</u> are simpler to use and reduce the number of injections required, as both <u>types of insulin</u> are combined into one injection.




### Intensive insulin therapy [[28]](/library/Tud6q70)[[29]](/library/Uudbq70)




This regimen provides optimal glycemic control as well as more flexibility in the daily diet and exercise plan, and it reduces the risk of complications of <u>diabetes</u> in patients with good adherence.




* Indications

* <u>T1DM</u>

* <u>T2DM</u> that cannot be sufficiently managed otherwise

* <u>Gestational diabetes mellitus</u>

* Full basal-bolus regimen: basal regimen with additional short-acting or <u>rapid-acting insulin</u> bolus before every major meal

* Insulin pump [[30]](/library/HicKGX0) 

* Insulin (usually a <u>rapid-acting insulin</u> analog) is subcutaneously infused through a small device attached to the <u>skin</u>.

* Basal rates and bolus insulin can be separately tailored to the patient's needs.

* May be beneficial in patients with <u>dawn phenomenon</u>





> [!TIP]
> The goal of <u>intensive insulin therapy</u> is to simulate physiological <u>glucose metabolism</u> (e.g., by keeping <u>fasting blood glucose</u> levels < 100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L) and <u>postprandial</u> blood <u>glucose</u> levels < 140 mg/dL (< 7.8 mmol/L).




### Full basal-bolus insulin regimen [[3]](/library/3HYSJq)[[31]](/library/hHYcJq)




* Calculate the total daily dose of insulin (TDD) needed.

* If the patient is already on a correction scale: Increase or decrease TDD by 10–20% as needed.

* If the patient is lean, has <u>T1DM</u>, is aged ≥ 70 years, and/or has a <u>GFR</u> < 60 mL/minute: 0.2–0.3 units/kg

* If none of the above criteria apply, use the blood <u>glucose</u> level:

* Blood <u>glucose</u> 140–200 mg/dL: 0.4 units/kg

* Blood <u>glucose</u> > 200 mg/dL: 0.5 units/kg

* Divide the TDD of insulin into basal insulin (50%) and prandial insulin (50%).

* Basal insulin: Administer as <u>long-acting insulin</u> (e.g., <u>glargine</u>) at bedtime.

* Prandial insulin: Administer as <u>rapid-acting insulin</u> (e.g., <u>lispro</u>) in equally divided doses before meals.

* Add <u>correction insulin therapy</u>.
1. * Take 5% of the TDD (e.g., 5% of a 60 unit TDD is 3 units); round down to the nearest whole number dose if necessary.
2. * Increase the prandial insulin dose by this increment for every 40 mg/dL above the glycemic target of 140 mg/dL.

* Adjust as needed.

* If <u>fasting</u> or mean <u>glucose</u> persistently > 140 mg/dL and no episodes of <u>hypoglycemia</u>: Increase basal insulin by 20%.

* If <u>fasting</u> or premeal <u>glucose</u> persistently > 140 mg/dL and no episodes of <u>hypoglycemia</u>: Increase prandial insulin by 2 units.

* In case of <u>hypoglycemia</u> < 70 mg/dL: Reduce basal insulin by 20% and/or prandial insulin by 2 units.





> [!TIP]
> Patients on a full basal-bolus regimen require intensive education, high motivation, and commitment, as this is the most complex and time-consuming <u>treatment for diabetes</u> and has an increased risk for <u>hypoglycemia</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Decrease or hold prandial insulin if the patient is <u>NPO</u>.




#### Principles of insulin adjustment




* Preprandial <u>glucose</u>

* Mainly affected by the basal insulin dose

* Daily <u>capillary</u> early morning measurements and measurements before applying an insulin dose are advised.

* <u>Postprandial</u> <u>glucose</u> is mainly affected by meal intake and prandial insulin dose.

* Certain conditions require temporary insulin adjustments.

* Increased insulin demand

* Illness

* <u>Stress</u>

* Decreased insulin demand

* Physical exercise: Increase <u>carbohydrate</u> intake and/or reduce prandial and/or basal insulin either before or after exercise. [[21]](/library/4dX3JC)[[32]](/library/qH1CrR0)

* Moderate intensity exercise: Reduce 50% of meal insulin.

* High intensity exercise: Reduce 75% of meal insulin.

* Patients on multiple daily insulin injections: Reduce daily basal insulin by 20% on the day of exercise.  [[32]](/library/qH1CrR0)

* Encourage <u>glucose</u> self-monitoring to reach appropriate insulin reduction and/or need for snacks.

* <u>Vomiting</u> and <u>diarrhea</u>: can lead to decreased <u>glucose</u> uptake, increasing the risk of <u>hypoglycemia</u>

* <u>Fasting</u>, e.g., for <u>surgery</u> (see “<u>Preoperative medication management</u>” and “<u>Fasting guidelines for elective surgery</u>.”)





### Correction insulin therapy [[2]](/library/UIWbX50)[[3]](/library/3HYSJq)




* Rapid-acting or <u>regular insulin</u> that is administered before meals (based on the premeal blood <u>glucose</u> level) or every 4–6 hours (in patients who are not eating).

* Used alone or in combination with scheduled <u>insulin therapy</u>.





| Blood <u>glucose</u> (mg/dL) | Insulin units |  |
| --- | --- | --- |
| <br>Patient eating all or most of each meal<br> | <br>Patient not eating<br> |  |
| < 70 | 0; Administer <u>hypoglycemia</u> protocol. | 0; Administer <u>hypoglycemia</u> protocol. |
| 71–140 | 0 | 0 |
| 141–180 | 4 | 2 |
| 181–220 | 6 | 4 |
| 221–260 | 8 | 6 |
| 261–300 mg/dL | 10 | 8 |





> [!WARNING]
> If blood <u>glucose</u> is < 70 mg/dL, hold all insulin and administer measures to control <u>hypoglycemia</u>.




### Sliding-scale insulin regimen [[3]](/library/3HYSJq)




* Description: rapid-acting or <u>short-acting insulin</u> used to treat a given level of <u>hyperglycemia</u> and often given independent of food intake, prior insulin administration, or <u>insulin sensitivity</u>

* <u>Correction insulin therapy</u> is typically preferred; institutional standards should be followed.

* Sliding-scale regimens alone should not be used for the long-term <u>management of diabetes</u>.





> [!TIP]
> Use of sliding scale <u>insulin therapy</u> alone without basal insulin is discouraged in the inpatient setting. [[33]](/library/gFdFh70)




### Insulin regimens for glucocorticoid-induced hyperglycemia




* <u>Basal-bolus insulin regimen</u> (preferred) 

* Consider splitting the total daily dose 30% <u>long-acting insulin</u> and 70% prandial <u>short-acting insulin</u>.

* Patients usually require about 0.4 units/kg/day but in patients receiving <u>dexamethasone</u>, insulin doses as high as 1.0–1.2 units/kg/day may be necessary. [[34]](/library/wHYhsq)

* The total required insulin dosage depends on individual patient factors (e.g., prior <u>insulin sensitivity</u>) and the <u>potency</u> of the <u>steroid</u>.

* <u>Correction insulin therapy</u>: may be adequate for short-term management

* Weight-based <u>NPH insulin</u> regimen

* Convert <u>glucocorticoid</u> to equivalent <u>prednisone</u> dose.

* Calculate daily <u>NPH</u> dose based on weight and <u>prednisone</u> dose equivalent.

* Administer <u>glucocorticoid</u> with <u>NPH</u> as a single dose in the morning.

* Consider adding basal insulin if the patient is on long-acting <u>glucocorticoids</u>.

* Adjust insulin doses (e.g., <u>correction insulin</u>) if the patient is on high-dose <u>glucocorticoids</u>.





| Weight-based <u>NPH insulin</u> for <u>glucocorticoid-induced hyperglycemia</u> |  |
| --- | --- |
| <u>Prednisone</u> dose equivalent (mg/day) | <u>NPH</u> (units/kg/day) |
| 10 | 0.1 |
| 20 | 0.2 |
| 30 | 0.3 |
| ≥ 40 | 0.4 |





### Insulin regimens for enteral and parenteral nutrition




#### Basal-bolus <u>insulin therapy</u> for patients receiving <u>enteral nutrition</u> [[33]](/library/gFdFh70)




* For patients already on insulin: Continue prior basal dose.

* Patients receiving continuous enteral feedings

* Prandial insulin

* 1 unit of insulin per 10–15 g of <u>carbohydrates</u> per day

* Administer as <u>NPH</u> every 8–12 hours or <u>regular insulin</u> every 6 hours.

* <u>Correction insulin</u>: Administer <u>rapid-acting insulin</u> (e.g., <u>lispro</u>) every 4 hours or <u>regular insulin</u> every 6 hours.

* Patients receiving bolus feedings

* Prandial insulin

* 1 unit of insulin per 10–15 g of <u>carbohydrates</u> per meal

* Administer as <u>rapid-acting insulin</u> (e.g., <u>lispro</u>) or <u>regular insulin</u> before each feeding.

* <u>Correction insulin</u>: Administer <u>rapid-acting insulin</u> before every meal.

* Start a dextrose infusion to prevent <u>hypoglycemia</u> if <u>enteral nutrition</u> is interrupted.

* Adjust as needed to glycemic targets, changes in medication, and changes in nutrition.





> [!WARNING]
> Abrupt discontinuation of <u>enteral feeding</u> in patients receiving insulin can result in <u>hypoglycemia</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Patients with <u>T1DM</u> require basal insulin even if feeding is discontinued.




#### <u>Insulin therapy</u> for patients receiving <u>total parenteral nutrition</u> (<u>TPN</u>)  [[33]](/library/gFdFh70)[[35]](/library/DHY1sq)




* Add <u>regular insulin</u> to IV <u>parenteral nutrition</u> solution. 

* Patients with <u>diabetes</u>: 1 unit per 10 g dextrose

* Patients without <u>diabetes</u>: 0.5 units per 10 g dextrose

* Add <u>correction insulin</u>: Administer as <u>short-acting insulin</u> (e.g., <u>regular insulin</u>) every 6 hours or <u>rapid-acting insulin</u> (e.g., <u>lispro</u>) every 4 hours.

* Adapt protocol to glycemic targets, changes in medication, and changes in nutrition.





> [!TIP]
> In patients with <u>glucocorticoid-induced hyperglycemia</u> who are already receiving insulin, administer <u>NPH insulin</u> in addition to the patient's usual <u>basal insulin regimen</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Consider using <u>glargine</u> or <u>detemir</u> in patients receiving <u>dexamethasone</u>. <u>Dexamethasone</u> has a longer <u>hyperglycemic</u> effect than <u>prednisone</u> and most other commonly used <u>systemic glucocorticoids</u>.
